'''Helen Murray Free''' (February 20, 1923 – May 1, 2021) was an American chemist and educator. She is most known for her work on in vitro self-testing systems for diabetes and other diseases.

==Early life and education==
Free was born in [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]], on February 20, 1923. Her father, James S. Murray, worked as a coal company salesman; her mother, Daisy Piper Murray, died during an influenza epidemic when Free was six.<ref name=CHFOralHistory /><ref name="NYT obit">{{cite news|title=Helen Murray Free Dies at 98; Chemist Developed Diabetes Test|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/05/03/science/helen-murray-free-dead.html|first=Denise|last=Gellene|date=May 3, 2021|access-date=May 3, 2021|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>

Free received her early education from the public schools in [[Youngstown, Ohio]], and graduated in 1941 as the [[valedictorian]] of [[Poland Seminary High School]]. While attending a summer camp at the [[College of Wooster]], she set her heart on attending Wooster. Greatly influenced by her high school English teacher, she originally intended to major in English and Latin in hopes of becoming a teacher; however, these plans soon changed. In December 1941 when [[Attack on Pearl Harbor|Pearl Harbor was bombed]], many young men either enlisted or were drafted into the army. As a result of the vacancy within "male-dominated disciplines",<ref name="acs.org">{{Cite web |title=Helen M. Free |url=https://www.acs.org/education/whatischemistry/women-scientists/helen-m-free.html |access-date=2024-10-25 |website=American Chemical Society |language=en}}</ref> women were encouraged to pursue careers in science. Consequently, Free switched her major to chemistry in which she obtained a [[Bachelor of Science]] in 1944.<ref name="NYT obit" /> She described her switch to chemistry as the “most terrific thing” that ever happened to her.<ref name=CHFOralHistory />

==Career==
Upon graduating from Wooster, Free immediately began working as a quality control chemist for [[Miles Laboratories]] (known as the creators of [[Alka-Seltzer]]), which involved testing the quality of ingredients in the company's line of vitamins.<ref name="acs.org" /> When Alfred Free had a position open in his biochemistry research group, she interviewed and filled the position.<ref name=HelenAlfredCHF>{{cite web|title=Helen M. Free and Alfred Free|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/helen-and-alfred-free|publisher=Science History Institute|access-date=February 19, 2018}}</ref> Little did she know that they would become lifelong research partners.<ref name="acs.org" /> They would marry two years later in 1947.<ref name="acs.org" />

Originally they researched different antibiotics before they moved on to dry reagent systems. The first thing Alfred and his team were tasked with was further refining [[Clinitest]] to make it more sensitive.<ref name="acs.org" /> Clinitest was a tablet that measured glucose levels in the urine of diabetic patients when a diluted solution of urine was subject to a tablet. A resulting color change would be able to determine the corresponding glucose levels of the patient. The team also developed the [[Acetest]], another tablet test for diabetes.<ref name=HelenAlfredCHF /><ref name=NWHF /> Continuing with this trend of enabling clinical tests to be carried out in tablet form, the team created Ictotest, which tested for [[hepatitis A]]. This test was able to chemically detect the presence of bilirubin in urine, which was indicative of carrying the disease.<ref name="sciencehistory.org">{{Cite web |title=Helen M. Free and Alfred Free |url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/education/scientific-biographies/helen-and-alfred-free/ |access-date=2024-10-25 |website=Science History Institute |language=en-US}}</ref>

The Frees introduced [[Clinistrip|Clinistix]] (the famous “dip-and-read” test) in 1956. It was the first dip-and-read diagnostic test strip for monitoring glucose in urine.<ref name=NWHF /> They then worked to develop other strips that could test for key indicators of diseases, such as proteins and ketones.<ref name="Diagnostic Test Strips 2010">{{Cite web |title=Al and Helen Free and the Development of Diagnostic Test Strips |url=https://www.acs.org/education/whatischemistry/landmarks/diagnosticteststrips.html |access-date=2024-10-25 |website=American Chemical Society |language=en}}</ref> Eventually, they were able to create Multistix, which enabled a urine analysis that combined multiple tests into one strip.<ref name="sciencehistory.org" /> They did this by making an impermeable barrier between the multiple reagents on the strip.<ref name="Diagnostic Test Strips 2010" /> Several other testing strips were developed and added to the market, including Uristix, Ketostix, Dextrostix, Labstix, and the still-current product, Multistix.<ref name=HelenAlfredCHF /><ref name=CHFOralHistory />

Free moved into the Growth and Development Department in 1969, and she eventually became the director of Specialty Test Systems seven years later. She was Director of Marketing Services for the Research Products Division when Bayer Diagnostics acquired Miles in 1978.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.uakron.edu/law/ip/council/profile.dot?identity=738916 |title=Helen M. Free |publisher=Uakron.edu |date=July 21, 2006 |access-date=November 17, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101021234115/http://www.uakron.edu/law/ip/council/profile.dot?identity=738916 |archive-date=October 21, 2010 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://jchemed.chem.wisc.edu/JCEWWW/features/eChemists/Bios/free.html |title=JCE Online: Biographical Snapshots: Snapshot |publisher=Jchemed.chem.wisc.edu |access-date=May 9, 2009}}</ref>

Free also earned a [[Master of Arts]] in management (health care administration) from [[Central Michigan University]] (1978), and served as an adjunct professor of management at [[Indiana University South Bend]].<ref name="invent1">{{cite web|url=http://web.mit.edu/invent/iow/free.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030318220315/http://web.mit.edu/invent/iow/free.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=March 18, 2003 |title=Inventor of the Week: Archive |publisher=Web.mit.edu |access-date=May 9, 2009}}</ref>

By 1975, Free had earned seven patents for her improvements in medical and clinical urinalysis testing. In that year, she and her husband co-authored their second book, ''Urinalysis in Laboratory Practice'', which is still a standard work in the field.<ref name="invent1" /> She retired in 1982, but continued to work as a consultant for Bayer Diagnostics in [[Elkhart, Indiana]].<ref name="NYT obit" />

===Later years===
After her retirement, Free became an active promoter of science education. She devoted special attention to educating both female and underprivileged students, through programs such as "Kids & Chemistry" and "Expanding Your Horizons."<ref name=NWHF>{{cite web|title=Helen Murray Free |url=http://dev.greatwomen.org/women-of-the-hall/search-the-hall-results/details/2/245-Free |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141216012920/http://dev.greatwomen.org/women-of-the-hall/search-the-hall-results/details/2/245-Free |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 16, 2014 |website=National Women's Hall of Fame |access-date=December 15, 2014 }}</ref>

==Personal life==
In 1947 she married Alfred Free, a fellow researcher in urinalysis. Together, they had six children: Eric, Kurt, Jake, Bonnie, Nina, and Penny. Also, she helped raise three stepchildren: Charles, Jane and Barb.<ref name="NYT obit" />

Free died on May 1, 2021, at a hospice facility in Elkhart at 98 from complications of a stroke.<ref name="NYT obit" />

===Awards and honors===
In 1980, Free received the [[Garvan–Olin Medal]], given to women for distinguished service in the field of chemistry.<ref name=CHFOralHistory>{{cite book|first=James J. |last=Bohning|title=Helen Murray Free, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by James J. Bohning at Elkhart, Indiana on 14 December, 1998 |date=December 14, 1998 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/free_hm_0176_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] }}</ref> In 1996, she received the [[Kilby International Awards|Kilby Award]] for lifetime achievement.<ref name=Kilby>{{cite web|title=The Kilby International Awards|url=http://www.kilby.org/kl_past_laureates.html|publisher=The Kilby International Awards Foundation|access-date=December 15, 2014}}</ref>

Free served as president of the [[American Association for Clinical Chemistry]] in 1990. Sixteen years later, she received its prestigious award for Outstanding Contributions to Clinical Chemistry.<ref name=AWCS1900>{{cite book|last1=Wayne|first1=Tiffany K.|title=American women of science since 1900|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|location=Santa Barbara, Calif.|isbn=978-1598841589|pages=407–408|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gPGZJ_YuMwgC&pg=PA408}}</ref>

Free was elected president of the [[American Chemical Society]] in 1993.<ref name=AWCS1900 /> The ACS named an award in her honor, the Helen M. Free Award for Public Outreach.<ref name=AWCS1900 /><ref name=ACSAward>{{cite web|title=Helen M. Free Award for Public Outreach|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/other/public/helenmfreeawardforpublicoutreach.html|website=ACS Chemistry for Life|publisher=American Chemical Society|access-date=December 15, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Award website |url=https://www.acs.org/funding/awards/helen-free-award-for-public-outreach.html}}</ref>

Free was inducted into the [[National Inventor's Hall of Fame]] in 2000.<ref name=Oakes2007>{{cite book|last1=Oakes|first1=Elizabeth H.|title=Encyclopedia of world scientists|date=2007|publisher=Facts on File|location=New York|isbn=9781438118826|pages=250–251|edition=Rev.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uPRB-OED1bcC&pg=PA251|access-date=December 15, 2014}}</ref> She was awarded the [[National Medal of Technology and Innovation]] a decade later by [[Barack Obama]].<ref>{{cite news|first=Debra |last=Daniel |title=Obama to present medal to Elkhart woman |url=http://www.wsbt.com/news/wsbt-obama-will-present-medal-to-el-111610,0,4078286.story |publisher=[[WSBT-TV]] |date=November 16, 2010 |access-date=November 17, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723235827/http://www.wsbt.com/news/wsbt-obama-will-present-medal-to-el-111610%2C0%2C4078286.story |archive-date=July 23, 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Obama|first=Barack|title=Remarks by the President in Presenting National Medals of Science and National Medals of Technology and Innovation|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2010/11/17/remarks-president-presenting-national-medals-science-and-national-medals|via=[[NARA|National Archives]]|work=[[whitehouse.gov]]|date=November 17, 2010 |access-date=November 17, 2010}}</ref><ref name=Paiva>{{cite journal|last1=Paiva|first1=Rini|title=News & Views: Helen Free Receives National Honor|journal=Clinical Chemistry|volume=57|date=2011|issue=Special Issue|pages=647–648|doi=10.1373/clinchem.2011.162859|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The work of Helen and Al Free in developing diagnostic test strips was designated a [[National Historic Chemical Landmarks|National Historic Chemical Landmark]] by the American Chemical Society on May 1, 2010, at the ETHOS Science Center in Elkhart, Indiana.<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/education/whatischemistry/landmarks/diagnosticteststrips.html|title = Al and Helen Free and the Development of Diagnostic Test Strips|date = May 1, 2010|access-date = July 12, 2014|website = National Historic Chemical Landmarks|publisher = American Chemical Society}}</ref> She was inducted into the [[National Women's Hall of Fame]] one year later.<ref>[https://www.womenofthehall.org/inductee/helen-murray-free/ National Women's Hall of Fame, Helen Murray Free]</ref>
